caveats: **Configuration as written, not the policy the OS evaluates.** Drop-ins, includes, other PAM services, sudoers includes and `/etc/audit/rules.d` are not followed, so a row shows that a setting exists, not that it is enforced. A PAM row shows the module by file name only, so a module loaded from a non-standard directory reads like the stock one. The macOS capture is a global policy from an unmanaged Mac, so on an MDM-managed device `policies|none` must not be read as "no lockout enforced".

**Windows `audit_policy` is the legacy categories only.** A `none` means the legacy `[Event Audit]` category is unset, not that the host is not auditing, because Advanced Audit Policy subcategories (the Windows 10/11 default and the norm under group policy) are not read and the OS may ignore a legacy value when "Force audit policy subcategory settings" is set. The export is the local security database without `/mergedpolicy`, so domain-joined behaviour is unmeasured.

**`lockout_keys|not_found` is not a verdict that lockout is off.** A host that enforces lockout through an unread place (an include, another PAM service, IdM or SSSD, `fail2ban`, or `faillog -m`, whose threshold lives in `/var/log/faillog`) still reports it. It is also written when no PAM file was read at all (a minimal image where only `login.defs` or `faillock.conf` is readable), so check the `source` list for which files were read; a PAM file saved with CRLF line endings is read with the carriage return trimmed, so a `pam_faillock` line that libpam would refuse to load can still read as configured.

**Windows is measured once and stages a full policy export on disk.** It was measured only as LocalSystem on a standalone host with the default `agent.data_dir`; the required privilege, the `NT SERVICE\YuzuAgent` account, domain-joined behaviour and a non-default data directory (an SMB share, a non-NTFS volume, a path over `MAX_PATH`, which may fail as `dest_dir_acl` or `secedit:exit_<n>`) are unmeasured. The staged copy holds the whole `SECURITYPOLICY` area and outlives a crash until a later Windows dispatch sweeps it, indefinitely if none follows, and an uninstall that keeps the data directory keeps it too.

**Root-only files read `unreadable` for an unprivileged agent, and a container reports its own `/etc`.** `sudoers`, `sudoers.d` and `audit.rules` need root or a read-override capability and are then an `unreadable` row, never an empty list. The sudoers sources are read without following symlinks and must be root-owned and not group/other-writable, so a symlinked `/etc/sudoers` (NixOS and some configuration-management layouts) reports `unreadable` with `symlink_refused`, while PAM files, which are legitimately symlinked (authselect), and the other sources are still followed. The shipped `Dockerfile.agent` image runs unprivileged with no host `/etc`, so it reports the image's files, as does the committed Linux sample.

definitions.description: Reports the local audit policy. Linux reads /etc/audit/audit.rules and reports rule, watch-rule and syscall-rule counts, lines it does not model, and the -e state (enabled, disabled, immutable or unset), from the rule file only, not the live kernel rules; macOS reads /etc/security/audit_control, which is absent by default on current macOS (reported `absent`, not a failure); Windows reports every [Event Audit] category from one `secedit /export` as none, success, failure or success_failure. Those are the LEGACY audit categories: where Advanced Audit Policy subcategories are in force -- the Windows 10/11 default and the norm under GPO -- they are not the effective audit state, so a category reading none means the legacy category is unset, NOT that the host is not auditing, and a legacy category reading success_failure may be ignored by the OS when the "Force audit policy subcategory settings" override (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy) is set, as many baselines do. `auditpol /get /category:*` is the effective state and is not read. audit.rules is 0640 root, so an unprivileged Linux agent reports `unreadable` and PERMISSION_DENIED. In a container the Linux file is the image's, not the host's.

Reports the local account lockout policy as one row per setting. Linux reads the lockout keys of login.defs, faillock.conf and the auth- and account-type lines of the pam_faillock, pam_tally2 and pam_tally modules in /etc/pam.d/common-auth, common-account, system-auth and password-auth (in a container these are the image's files, not the host's); macOS reads the authentication policies from `pwpolicy -getaccountpolicies` (no authentication policy reports `policies|none`, the default); Linux reports `lockout_keys|not_found` when at least one source was read and no lockout key was found, a statement about the files read and not a verdict that lockout is off; Windows reads LockoutBadCount, ResetLockoutCount and LockoutDuration from one `secedit /export` staged under agent.data_dir and removed on return. It reports configuration, not live lockout counters; on Windows that is the LOCAL security database only (no /mergedpolicy), so on a domain-joined host the GPO-effective policy is not reported, and it has been measured only as LocalSystem on a standalone host. A source the OS reports missing reads `absent`; one that could not be read reads `unreadable` with a reason and downgrades the result, never an empty success. Keys are each OS's own vocabulary and are deliberately NOT normalised across platforms, so a fleet-wide comparison must branch per OS.

Reports the local password policy as one row per setting: which setting, its value and where it was read. Linux reads login.defs, pwquality.conf and the password-type lines of the pam_pwquality, pam_pwhistory, pam_cracklib and pam_unix modules in /etc/pam.d/common-password, system-auth and password-auth (in a container these are the image's files, not the host's); macOS reads the global account policies from `pwpolicy -getaccountpolicies`; Windows reads MinimumPasswordAge, MaximumPasswordAge, MinimumPasswordLength, PasswordComplexity, PasswordHistorySize and ClearTextPassword from one `secedit /export` staged under agent.data_dir and removed on return. It reports what the configuration states, not the live PAM or LSA decision; on Windows that is the LOCAL security database only (no /mergedpolicy), so on a domain-joined host the GPO-effective policy is not reported, and it has been measured only as LocalSystem on a standalone host. A source the OS reports missing reads `absent`; one that could not be read reads `unreadable` with a reason and downgrades the result to CONSTRAINED (PERMISSION_DENIED only when every read was refused and nothing was readable), never an empty success. Keys are each OS's own vocabulary and are deliberately NOT normalised across platforms (Windows MinimumPasswordLength, Linux PASS_MIN_LEN or pwquality minlen, macOS minimum_length all state a minimum length), so a fleet-wide comparison must branch per OS.

Reports the parsed content of /etc/sudoers and every file in /etc/sudoers.d, one row per Defaults line, alias, include directive or user spec. Include directives are listed, not followed; a line the parser does not recognise is kind `unmodelled` with the raw line, never dropped; a file sudo would skip by name is kind `ignored`. Aliases and includes are not resolved, and `nopasswd` reflects the NOPASSWD tag only. The sources are opened without following symlinks and must be root-owned and not group/other-writable (else `unreadable` with symlink_refused or insecure_owner_or_mode, so a symlinked sudoers file, as on NixOS, is not read). Reading /etc/sudoers needs root or the file's group (0440), so an unprivileged agent reports kind `unreadable` and PERMISSION_DENIED when nothing else was readable (CONSTRAINED otherwise), never an empty list. Values pass the shared output escaper, which renders a literal backslash as `/` (so `%domain\ admins` reads `%domain/ admins`). A User_List, Host_List or run-as over 4 KiB, or a line expanding to more than 256 rows, is not decoded and is one `unmodelled` row with its raw text. In a container these are the image's files, not the host's. Linux and macOS only; Windows has no sudoers.

description: Reports local password, lockout and audit policy posture and sudoers content
how_it_works:
Four read-only actions report a host's local security configuration, one question each: `password_policy` (password rules), `lockout_policy` (account lockout), `audit_policy` (audit configuration) and `sudoers` (who may run commands as another user). None takes parameters, so no request text reaches a path or a command line, and no host policy is ever configured, imported or applied. Linux reads configuration files. macOS reads files for `audit_policy` and `sudoers` and runs `pwpolicy -getaccountpolicies` for password and lockout policy. Windows runs `secedit /export` once, stages the export in a private scratch directory under `agent.data_dir`, parses it and deletes it; `sudoers` does not exist on Windows. Every source reads as a **value**, as **`absent`** (the OS definitively says the file, key or directory is not there) or as **`unreadable`** (the read failed), and a failed read never looks like an absent one. The rows describe configuration as written, not the policy the OS evaluates.

### What is read, in what order

| Action | Linux (files, in read order) | macOS | Windows |
|---|---|---|---|
| `password_policy` | `/etc/login.defs` (7 keys: `PASS_MAX_DAYS`, `PASS_MIN_DAYS`, `PASS_MIN_LEN`, `PASS_WARN_AGE`, `ENCRYPT_METHOD`, `SHA_CRYPT_MIN_ROUNDS`, `SHA_CRYPT_MAX_ROUNDS`), then `/etc/security/pwquality.conf` (every key), then the `password` lines of `pam_pwquality`, `pam_pwhistory`, `pam_cracklib` and `pam_unix` in `/etc/pam.d/common-password`, `system-auth` and `password-auth` | `pwpolicy -getaccountpolicies`, parsed with `CFPropertyListCreateWithData`; password categories only | one `secedit /export`; the six `[System Access]` keys `MinimumPasswordAge`, `MaximumPasswordAge`, `MinimumPasswordLength`, `PasswordComplexity`, `PasswordHistorySize`, `ClearTextPassword` |
| `lockout_policy` | `/etc/login.defs` (4 login-prompt keys: `LOGIN_RETRIES`, `LOGIN_TIMEOUT`, `FAILLOG_ENAB`, `FAIL_DELAY`), then `/etc/security/faillock.conf` (every key), then the `auth` and `account` lines of `pam_faillock`, `pam_tally2` and `pam_tally` in `common-auth`, `common-account`, `system-auth` and `password-auth` | the same `pwpolicy` run; authentication categories only | the same export; `LockoutBadCount`, `ResetLockoutCount`, `LockoutDuration` |
| `audit_policy` | `/etc/audit/audit.rules`: counts of rules, watch rules, syscall rules, unmodelled lines and control lines, plus the `-e` state | `/etc/security/audit_control`, one row per `key:value` line (the file is absent by default) | the same export; one row per legacy `[Event Audit]` category the export carries |
| `sudoers` | `/etc/sudoers`, then each file in `/etc/sudoers.d` in name order (names containing a dot or ending in `~` are listed as `ignored`, as sudo skips them) | the same | not supported: one `unsupported` row |

**What is deliberately not read.**

- **Linux:** `pwquality.conf.d` fragments, `faillock.conf` drop-ins, PAM `@include` and substack targets, PAM services other than the named files (`sshd`, `login`), `/etc/audit/rules.d`, the live kernel audit rules (`auditctl -l`), IdM or SSSD policy, `fail2ban`, and sudoers `include` targets (listed, not followed).
- **macOS:** per-user policy (only the global account policy is read) and any policy delivered by a configuration profile; the capture was taken on an unmanaged Mac.
- **Windows:** Advanced Audit Policy subcategories (`auditpol`), the effective domain policy (the export is the local security database, without `/mergedpolicy`), and every part of the export beyond the keys above. The privilege-right assignments and registry values in the export are staged on disk but never reported.

### Reading rules

- **One token per failure.** Each failure adds one token, `<source>:<cause>`; the Windows scratch-directory tokens (`data_dir_unset`, `dest_dir_*`) keep the spelling used by the sibling `execution_artifacts` plugin. An `absent` source adds no token and does not lower the status.
- **Status.** `PERMISSION_DENIED` only when at least one read was refused, no source was readable and nothing else failed. A refusal next to any readable source, and every other failure, is `CONSTRAINED`. So a Linux `sudoers` refusal next to a readable `/etc/sudoers.d` file is `CONSTRAINED`.
- **Unrecognised values are named.** A value the tables cannot interpret is `unmodelled`, never dropped.
- **Silent by design.** These produce no row and no token: one absent PAM file while a sibling alternative exists (only all-absent is a `source_state|absent|/etc/pam.d` row); a file that was read but sets none of the reported keys (Debian's all-commented `faillock.conf`, a PAM file with no matching module line), apart from the Linux `lockout_policy` case below; a PAM line that is not `type control module`; `login.defs` keys outside the per-action list; `pwpolicy` element keys other than `policyIdentifier`, `policyContent` and `policyParameters`; and a Windows `[Event Audit]` category the export omits.
- **Not silent.** A `pwpolicy` element that carries none of the reportable keys is a `source_state|unreadable:missing_content` row.
- **macOS plist items.** Anything not in the documented shape is a `source_state|unreadable:<defect>` row with a `pwpolicy:<defect>` token, never dropped and never `policies|none`. A `policyAttribute*` parameter is its own key; any other scalar parameter (for example `autoEnableInSeconds`, the lockout duration) is `unmodelled_parameter` with the value `<name>=<value>`.
- **Linux `lockout_policy` with no key found.** Written as `lockout_policy|lockout_keys|not_found|<files>` when at least one source was read and no key row resulted. The decision is in the diagram below; `<files>` lists exactly the files read successfully, comma-separated, in read order.

### What you can decide with it

| Question | Action | What you get | When you get nothing useful |
|---|---|---|---|
| Is a minimum password length, complexity, history or maximum age set? | `password_policy` | Windows: the six `secedit` keys as raw numbers. macOS: Apple policy expressions as `policy_content` rows plus a derived `minimum_length`. Linux: `login.defs` aging keys, `pwquality.conf` keys such as `minlen`, and the PAM `password` lines | A key the Windows export lacks reads `absent`. An unmanaged Mac reports little (the captured sample shows only the FileVault policy). On Linux a setting held in an unread place is invisible |
| Is account lockout configured? | `lockout_policy` | Windows: `LockoutBadCount`, `ResetLockoutCount`, `LockoutDuration`. macOS: authentication policy rows, or `policies\|none`. Linux: `faillock.conf` keys (for example `deny`, `unlock_time`) and PAM `pam_faillock`, `pam_tally2` or `pam_tally` lines | Linux `lockout_keys\|not_found` and macOS `policies\|none` mean nothing was found in what was read, not that lockout is off |
| Is auditing configured? | `audit_policy` | Windows: legacy category settings (`none`, `success`, `failure`, `success_failure`). macOS: `audit_control` lines. Linux: rule counts and the `-e` state of the rules file (`enabled`, `disabled`, `immutable`, or `unset`) | Windows `none` means the legacy category is unset, not that the host is not auditing. macOS reports `absent` by default. Linux does not show live kernel rules |
| Who can become root, and without a password? | `sudoers` | `user_spec` rows with subject, run-as and a `nopasswd` flag; `defaults`, `alias`, `include` and `includedir` rows alongside | Windows has no sudoers. Read a `defaults` row with `!authenticate` together with `nopasswd`, because it also makes matching grants passwordless |

- **Read it per OS.** Keys keep each OS's own vocabulary (`MinimumPasswordLength`, `PASS_MIN_LEN` or `minlen`, `minimum_length`), so a fleet baseline branches per OS. The plugin reports settings; it does not score them against a benchmark.
- **A row proves a setting exists, not that it is enforced.** `deny = 0` and `silent` are rows too. A clean `OK` status means every source was read or definitively absent; it does not mean the host meets a standard.
- **Orientation, not a mapping.** Password, lockout and audit settings are the inputs to checks in standards such as CIS Benchmarks and PCI DSS; this plugin was not built to certify against either.

### Diagrams

#### Windows export lifecycle

The export is the whole security-policy area, so it is staged only in a directory the agent created, owns and holds open. The completeness check stops a truncated file from reporting the keys it lost as `absent`. A crash between the export and the delete leaves the directory until a later Windows dispatch sweeps it.

#### Linux lockout_policy: when `not_found` is written

The four `login.defs` keys are reported as rows but do not count, because they are login-prompt and faillog settings rather than lockout counters. An absent or unreadable source keeps its own `source_state` row and does not suppress `not_found`; any key row does.

#### Status for the file and tool legs

On Windows every failure is `CONSTRAINED` with a `constrained|<token>` row, except `secedit:access_denied`, which is `PERMISSION_DENIED`. On macOS a failed `pwpolicy` run is always `CONSTRAINED`.

columns.description: The file the entry was read from; /etc/sudoers.d on a row about the directory listing itself; a dash on the row-cap marker.

columns.description: Entry kind. defaults, alias, include, includedir, user_spec: a recognised line. unmodelled: a line the parser has no interpretation for (raw line in commands); one that still carries a NOPASSWD: or PASSWD: tag the parser could not decode also adds the failure token <file>:undecoded_passwd_tag (CONSTRAINED). A user spec becomes one row per clause AND per change of run-as or NOPASSWD tag within a clause. Lines are lexed as sudo 1.9.16 lexes them (checked against sudo -ll), so a colon in a quoted value, an IPv6 host or a digest never splits a clause; the nopasswd column is the tag alone, and a line sudo itself rejects is best-effort. ignored: a sudoers.d file sudo skips by name (commands name_ignored_by_sudo). absent: the file or the /etc/sudoers.d directory does not exist. unreadable: the read failed (bare reason token in commands, e.g. permission_denied; truncated on the /etc/sudoers.d row when the listing hit its 256-entry cap; row_cap, with file -, on the marker row once output reaches 4096 rows). The plugin also emits kind unsupported on Windows (reason windows_has_no_sudoers in commands), which this definition cannot surface because it does not run there.
columns.name: kind

columns.description: Who the entry applies to. A user spec carries <user>@<host> -- the user, group or alias joined to the host list the spec applies on; each colon-separated Host_List clause of one line is its own row. An alias row carries <Alias_Type>:<name>. A scoped Defaults line carries its scope (user:, host:, cmnd:, runas:). A dash when not applicable.
columns.name: subject

columns.description: Run-as user/group of a user spec; a dash when not applicable.
columns.name: runas

columns.description: Whether a user spec carries the NOPASSWD tag: true or false; a dash on a row that is not a user spec. It reflects the tag only: a Defaults row with !authenticate (kind defaults) also makes matching grants passwordless and must be read alongside it.
columns.name: nopasswd

columns.description: The command list of a user spec (any tag other than NOPASSWD/PASSWD, e.g. SETENV:, is kept in front of its command as TAG: , and any Option_Spec such as CWD=/tmp or TIMEOUT=5m verbatim), the Defaults or alias body, an include path, the raw text of an unmodelled line, the reason on an ignored or unreadable row, or a dash on an absent row.
columns.name: commands

outputs_note:
Pipe-delimited text rows, one per line of output. The first field is the fixed action name (`password_policy`, `lockout_policy`, `audit_policy` or `sudoers`), and every field passes through the shared untrusted-output escaper. A key present with no value reads `present`.

- **Settings rows.** `<action>|<key>|<value>|<source>`: the setting, its value and the file, `secedit` or `pwpolicy:<policy identifier>` it came from.
- **Source-state rows.** A missing or unreadable source is one `<action>|source_state|<state>|<source>` row, with state `absent` or `unreadable:<token>`. For `sudoers` the same fact is a row of kind `absent` (`commands` is `-`) or `unreadable` (`commands` is the bare token, for example `permission_denied`).
- **Windows.** `password_policy` and `lockout_policy` always emit their fixed key list, and a key the export lacks reads `absent`. `audit_policy` emits one row per `[Event Audit]` category the export carries (a real export has nine); an omitted category has no row. An export missing `[System Access]` or `[Event Audit]`, or not ending in the signed `[Version]` section, is `secedit:export_incomplete`. A section that is present but empty is `CONSTRAINED` with `secedit:section_missing_system_access` or `secedit:section_missing_event_audit`.
- **macOS.** `policies|none` is the default when no matching policy is set and no item was malformed. A plist item not in the documented shape is a `source_state|unreadable:<defect>` row whose source names the policy identifier or category (`pwpolicy` when neither is known).
- **Linux `lockout_policy`.** One `lockout_keys|not_found|<files>` row when sources were read and no key row resulted (see How it works).

**`sudoers` rows** are `sudoers|<file>|<kind>|<subject>|<runas>|<nopasswd>|<commands>`.

- **Splitting.** Each `:`-separated `Host_List = ...` clause of a user spec is its own row, and so is each change of run-as or `NOPASSWD` tag within a clause (`alice ALL = (root) NOPASSWD: /a, (bob) /b` is two rows). Option_Spec words (`CWD=`, `CHROOT=`, `TIMEOUT=`, `NOTBEFORE=`, `ROLE=`, `APPARMOR_PROFILE=` and so on) stay verbatim in `commands`, like every tag other than `NOPASSWD` and `PASSWD`.
- **Lexing.** Files are lexed as sudo 1.9.16 lexes them: a `:` inside a quoted value, an escape, an IPv6 host or a digest never splits a clause, and a `#` comment never continues onto the next line. The lexer was checked differentially against sudo 1.9.16; no test corpus or result is committed.
- **Fail-safe.** A line that still carries a `NOPASSWD:` or `PASSWD:` tag the parser could not decode is kind `unmodelled` plus the token `<file>:undecoded_passwd_tag` (`CONSTRAINED`).
- **Not covered.** `nopasswd` is the tag alone; aliases and includes are not resolved; another sudo version may lex differently; a line sudo itself rejects is reported best-effort.
- **Limits.** A `User_List`, `Host_List` or run-as over 4 KiB, or a line that would expand to more than 256 rows, is one `unmodelled` row with its raw text. Parsing stops at the row cap.
- **Escaping.** The shared escaper renders a literal backslash as `/` (`%domain\ admins` reads `%domain/ admins`); this is the platform's deliberately lossy output convention, not a sudoers rule.
- **NUL bytes.** A file holding a NUL byte is `unreadable:embedded_nul` as a whole (`<path>:embedded_nul`), because no value after it can be reported as the one in force. A Windows export holding one anywhere is `secedit:embedded_nul` with no rows.

**Row cap.** Every Linux and macOS action stops at 4096 rows per dispatch, or at 4 MiB of formatted output: 4095 data rows plus one marker row, and the status becomes `CONSTRAINED` with the token `row_cap`. The Windows leg has no row cap; its only bound is the 1 MiB export limit below.

- **Marker shapes.** File-backed Linux and macOS `audit_policy` sources write `<action>|source_state|unreadable:row_cap|<action>`; `sudoers` writes `sudoers|-|unreadable|-|-|-|row_cap`; the macOS `pwpolicy` path writes the four-field shape with the literal source `pwpolicy`.
- **Other bounds.** The `pwpolicy` path is also bounded by the tool's own output cap (`pwpolicy:output_truncated`), and a long policy identifier or category is cut to 256 bytes before it is repeated in each row's source field. The Windows export is bounded by the 1 MiB cap (`secedit:output_oversized`), which is the only bound on that leg's row count. The `/etc/sudoers.d` listing is capped at 256 entries (`sudoers.d:truncated`, row `sudoers|/etc/sudoers.d|unreadable|-|-|-|truncated`).

**Failure rows and return codes.**

- **No rows at all.** When a non-OK outcome produced no rows (today only a failed `pwpolicy` run: spawn error, deadline, cancelled, signalled or otherwise unexpected end, truncated output, non-zero exit, no plist or an unparseable one) the action writes one `<action>|status|constrained|<reason>` row, where the fourth field is the reason token. `status|permission_denied` exists only as a defensive branch that no current source reaches.
- **Return code 0.** File-backed and `pwpolicy` failures are data-level outcomes and return 0, as does every Windows failure (degradation is the typed status, not the return code). An unknown action name returns 1 with the single row `unknown action: <name>`.
- **Two-field `constrained` row.** Written by every Windows failure and by an exception contained on any OS (`constrained|internal_error`, return 1). On Windows it reads `constrained` even when the typed status is `PERMISSION_DENIED`; the status and the token (for example `secedit:access_denied`) carry the distinction.
- **`sudoers` on Windows.** Returns 1 with the row `sudoers|-|unsupported|-|-|-|windows_has_no_sudoers` and status `UNAVAILABLE`.

privileges.grant: `secedit /export` needs an elevated token. Which privilege is required, and whether the dedicated `NT SERVICE\YuzuAgent` account succeeds, are not measured. The one measured run had `SeSecurityPrivilege` present but in its default Disabled state
privileges.if_refused: A refused `secedit` run is expected to exit non-zero and report `CONSTRAINED` with `secedit:exit_<n>` (not measured). `PERMISSION_DENIED` with `secedit:access_denied` is reported only when the agent cannot open its own export file (never observed). Either way the action returns 0 with the row `constrained|<token>`
privileges.measured: LocalSystem, elevated, on a bare-metal standalone (not domain-joined) Windows 11 Pro host: a real 12,828-byte UTF-16LE export, and the committed sample captured 2026-09-30 (`docs/samples/windows.txt`). No fixture of the export is committed

privileges.grant: None for `pwpolicy -getaccountpolicies`; `/etc/sudoers` is `root:wheel` `0440`, which the root daemon can read
privileges.if_refused: `EACCES` on `/etc/sudoers` reports the row kind `unreadable` with `permission_denied` and the action reports `PERMISSION_DENIED`/`PARTIAL`; a failed `pwpolicy` run reports `CONSTRAINED` with `pwpolicy:<cause>`
privileges.measured: Bare-metal Mac, unprivileged (euid 501), sample captured 2026-09-29 (`docs/samples/macos.txt`). No root-privileged run has been captured, so the refused `sudoers` shape in the sample is what a normal user sees
privileges.runs_as: agent daemon, root today (LaunchDaemon carries no `UserName` key, `docs/agent-privilege-model.md` TL;DR)

privileges.grant: None for the world-readable config. `/etc/audit/audit.rules` (`0640`) and `/etc/sudoers` plus `/etc/sudoers.d/*` (`0440`) need root or a read-override capability. A file capability does not take effect under the packaged unit's `NoNewPrivileges=true` (verified for the sibling `remote_access_audit` plugin), so expect those files to read as refused unless read access is granted another way; not measured for this plugin
privileges.if_refused: `EACCES`/`EPERM` reports the source `unreadable` with `<path>:permission_denied`; the action reports `PERMISSION_DENIED` when nothing else was readable, otherwise `CONSTRAINED`; a missing file (`ENOENT`) reports `absent` with no token
privileges.measured: Only in a container: the sample (2026-09-30, `docs/samples/linux.txt`) is a run of the built `.so` as root in a Debian 13 container hardened for the capture (sudo with a `sudoers.d` drop-in, auditd rules, pwquality and faillock values), so it describes that container's `/etc`, not a host. No fixtures are committed and no bare-metal Linux host has been captured
privileges.runs_as: agent daemon, dedicated unprivileged account on the packaged unit (never root by design)

result_status.when: Every source was read or definitively `absent`. An absent source adds no token, so a default macOS host with no `audit_control` reports `OK`.

Linux and macOS file reads: at least one source failed for a reason other than a refusal, or a refusal while something else was readable; the reason lists one token per failure. `<path>` is the full path, including `/etc/sudoers.d/<name>` for a file in that directory; a failure to list the directory itself is `sudoers.d:<cause>` (the bare name `sudoers.d`, not the path). `dangling_symlink` is a path that is a symlink whose target does not exist or cannot be reached (for example an `authselect` PAM link mid-apply): it is a failed read, never the silent absent a missing PAM alternative gets. `symlink_refused` and `insecure_owner_or_mode` are the sudoers-only checks: those sources are opened without following links and must be owned by uid 0 and not group/other-writable (stricter than sudo, which allows a group-writable file owned by the sudoers group), so a planted link on a sudoers file never turns the action into a read of another file. Only the file itself is checked, not its parent directories.
macOS `password_policy` and `lockout_policy`: the `pwpolicy` run or its plist failed.

macOS `password_policy` and `lockout_policy`: the plist parsed but an item was not in the documented shape; each is also a `source_state|unreadable:<defect>` row, alongside every well-formed policy's rows.
Windows: the scratch directory or the `secedit` run or export failed; the action returns 0 (degradation is carried by the typed status) with the row `constrained|<token>`.
Any leg: an unexpected exception was contained in `execute()`; the action returns 1 with the row `constrained|internal_error`.

File legs: at least one read was refused, no source was readable and nothing else failed. Windows: the agent could not open its own export file (`ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`; never observed — a refused `secedit` run surfaces as `secedit:exit_<n>` instead).
`sudoers` dispatched on Windows; or any action on an OS with no leg (not a supported platform; row `constrained|unsupported_os`).

where_the_data_goes: **Instruction result.** Rows travel over the agent's mTLS gRPC channel as the command response and land in the ResponseStore, queryable at `/api/responses/{id}`. Each action is a gathered definition (`crossplatform.local_security_policy.<action>`, 300s TTL).
**Not consumed by** daily-sync, TAR, DEX, or metrics.

**Sensitivity.** Password, lockout and audit rows are a compliance baseline of the host (a short minimum length, no lockout, auditing off), which is useful to an attacker choosing a target. `sudoers` rows carry account and group names, run-as targets, `NOPASSWD` flags and command text verbatim (an argument can embed a secret), i.e. who may become root. The rows stay in the response store under its generic retention. With RBAC enforcement off, any authenticated session that can dispatch to the device can read them; the actions are `Security:Read`, not `UserManagement:Read`, because they sit with the other privilege-posture reads. Treat all four like other `Security` data.
**Siblings:** `firewall`, `bitlocker` and `antivirus` (other `Security` posture plugins) and `users` (account and group membership; this plugin reports policy, not accounts).
